LS.L6.PSW.T01.title: Positive self-esteem: body image
LS.L6.PSW.T01.description: Understanding and respecting body changes; influences on body image from media and society; acceptance of the self.
LS.L6.PSW.T01.recovery_strategy: All bodies are valuable. Counter media ideals with the truth that bodies are diverse and changes during puberty are normal. Never prescribe how a body should look.

questions.question: What is 'body image'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does body image mean?
options: How you see and feel about your own body
questions.expected: How you see and feel about your own body
questions.memo: Body image is your inner picture of your body — what you like, what you don't, how comfortable you feel in it.

questions.question: What is POSITIVE body image?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does positive body image look like?
options: Accepting and respecting your body for what it can do, not just how it looks
Comparing it to celebrities every day
questions.expected: Accepting and respecting your body for what it can do, not just how it looks
questions.memo: Positive body image isn't about thinking you're perfect — it's about respecting your body and being okay with it. Bodies are for living, not just looking.

questions.question: During puberty, bodies normally:
questions.ruby_prompt: During puberty, bodies normally:
options: Change in many ways — height, weight, hair, voice — at different times for different people
questions.expected: Change in many ways — height, weight, hair, voice — at different times for different people
questions.memo: Puberty changes everyone, but not at the same time or in the same way. Comparing your timing to others is unfair to yourself.

questions.question: True or false: All bodies in real life look like bodies in magazines and on social media.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: All bodies in real life look like the bodies you see in magazines and social media.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: Media bodies are edited, filtered, posed and often impossible. Real bodies are diverse and look different from media bodies.

questions.question: What does the MEDIA often do to images of bodies?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does the media often do to images of bodies?
options: Edit and filter them to make people look 'perfect'
Show them exactly as they are
questions.expected: Edit and filter them to make people look 'perfect'
questions.memo: Photoshop, filters, lighting, makeup, angles — media images are heavily produced. Comparing yourself to them is comparing yourself to a fake.

questions.question: Lerato feels bad after scrolling social media for an hour. The likely reason is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato feels bad about herself after an hour on social media. What's the likely reason?
options: Comparing herself to edited, posed photos that don't show real life
questions.expected: Comparing herself to edited, posed photos that don't show real life
questions.memo: Hours on social media linked to lower body satisfaction in many studies. Knowing this helps: take breaks, follow real-life accounts, remember it's curated.

questions.question: Which is a TRUTH about healthy bodies?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a truth about healthy bodies?
options: Healthy bodies come in many shapes, sizes, colours and abilities
Only one body type is healthy
Healthy means looking like a model
questions.expected: Healthy bodies come in many shapes, sizes, colours and abilities
questions.memo: Health shows up in energy, strength, mood, sleep, blood tests — not just appearance. Bodies are diverse and many are healthy.

questions.question: True or false: It's normal for your body to change a lot between ages 10 and 16.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: It's normal for your body to change a lot between ages 10 and 16.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — puberty stretches across years. Growth spurts, voice changes, hair, sweat, acne — all normal. Different bodies do this at different paces.

questions.question: Which is a way to build positive body image?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a way to build positive body image?
options: Focus on what your body can DO (run, hug, help) and surround yourself with kind voices
Stare at the mirror for hours
questions.expected: Focus on what your body can DO (run, hug, help) and surround yourself with kind voices
questions.memo: What your body does matters more than how it looks. Strong, kind, helpful, learning — these are real values. Choose friends who reflect that back.

questions.question: Mpho's friend keeps criticising her appearance. The healthiest response is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Mpho's friend keeps criticising her appearance. What's the healthiest response?
options: Tell her friend it hurts, set a boundary, and find friends who support her
questions.expected: Tell her friend it hurts, set a boundary, and find friends who support her
questions.memo: Friends who tear down your body image aren't healthy. Speaking up is fair. If they don't stop, change the company you keep.

questions.question: Why is it dangerous to diet harshly as a child?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it dangerous to diet harshly as a child or teenager?
options: Growing bodies need food. Harsh dieting can cause illness, eating disorders and lifelong harm
questions.expected: Growing bodies need food. Harsh dieting can cause illness, eating disorders and lifelong harm
questions.memo: Growing bodies need fuel. Cutting food severely can lead to eating disorders, which are serious illnesses. Healthy eating ≠ dieting.

questions.question: Where can a person get help for body image worries?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where can a young person get help for serious body image worries?
options: A school counsellor, a parent or trusted adult, a clinic, or Childline 116
questions.expected: A school counsellor, a parent or trusted adult, a clinic, or Childline 116
questions.memo: Body image worries that won't go away can become serious. Help is real — counsellors, doctors, parents. SADAG (0800 567 567) helps with mental health.

questions.question: True or false: Self-acceptance grows easier when you stop comparing yourself to others.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Self-acceptance grows easier when you stop comparing yourself to others.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — comparison is the thief of joy. Comparing yourself only to your past self leaves more room for self-acceptance.

questions.question: Karabo notices acne starting. The healthy attitude is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo notices acne starting. What's a healthy attitude?
options: Acne is normal during puberty — basic skincare and patience help, and a clinic can help if it's severe
She failed at being a teenager
questions.expected: Acne is normal during puberty — basic skincare and patience help, and a clinic can help if it's severe
questions.memo: Acne happens to most teens because of hormone changes. Gentle washing, not picking, and clinic help for severe cases. Not a moral failing.

questions.question: Tell me one thing your body lets you do that you appreciate.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one thing your body lets you do that you appreciate.
questions.expected: My body lets me run and play with my friends
questions.memo: Good answers: run, play, hug, learn, sing, dance, help, see, hear, hold a pencil, eat my favourite food. Bodies do incredible things.

questions.question: Sipho notices his voice is changing. This is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho notices his voice is starting to change. What's happening?
options: A normal part of puberty — his voice box is growing
questions.expected: A normal part of puberty — his voice box is growing
questions.memo: Voice changes are normal in puberty, especially for boys. The voice may crack for a while. It settles into its adult sound over months.

questions.question: True or false: People can have a healthy positive body image at any size or shape.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: People can have a healthy positive body image at any size or shape.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — body image is about your relationship with your body, not its measurements. Positive body image is for everyone.

questions.question: Put these in order for handling a bad body image day.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order for handling a day when you feel bad about your body.
options: Notice the feeling — name it ('I'm comparing again')
Put down social media for a while
Do something your body enjoys (walk, play, dance)
questions.expected: Notice the feeling — name it ('I'm comparing again'),Put down social media for a while,Do something your body enjoys (walk, play, dance),Talk to someone kind
questions.memo: Notice → unplug → move → connect. Strategy beats spiralling.

questions.question: Society's MESSAGES about bodies often:
questions.ruby_prompt: Society's messages about bodies often:
options: Push a narrow idea of beauty that doesn't fit most real people
questions.expected: Push a narrow idea of beauty that doesn't fit most real people
questions.memo: Most beauty messages aim to sell products. They make people feel inadequate so we'll buy. Knowing this changes how we receive the message.

questions.question: The most important truth about YOUR body is:
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the most important truth about your body?
options: It's yours, it's unique, and it deserves care and respect from you and others
It's the most important thing about you
It needs to look like a model
questions.expected: It's yours, it's unique, and it deserves care and respect from you and others
questions.memo: Your body is uniquely yours. Care for it, respect it, listen to it. It's the home you live in for your whole life — befriend it.

LS.L6.PSW.T02.title: Abilities, interests and potential
LS.L6.PSW.T02.description: Identifying own abilities, interests and potential; relationships between them; creating opportunities and action plans to develop them.
LS.L6.PSW.T02.recovery_strategy: Encourage the learner to notice their own strengths and dreams. Bridge to action — small steps make potential real.

questions.question: What is an 'ability'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is an ability?
options: Something you can do — a skill you have already developed
Something you hope to do one day
questions.expected: Something you can do — a skill you have already developed
questions.memo: Abilities are what you can do NOW — read, draw, run, code, calm a friend down. They are the skills you've built.

questions.question: What is an 'interest'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is an interest?
options: Something you enjoy or find fascinating
questions.expected: Something you enjoy or find fascinating
questions.memo: Interests are what pull you in — music, sports, animals, computers, science. They give clues to careers and joy.

questions.question: What is 'potential'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is potential?
options: What you could become or do with practice and opportunity
questions.expected: What you could become or do with practice and opportunity
questions.memo: Potential is your future possibility. It's not fixed — it grows as you learn, try and get opportunities.

questions.question: How are abilities, interests and potential related?
questions.ruby_prompt: How are abilities, interests and potential related?
options: Interests pull you toward an area; abilities are what you build; potential is what you could become
questions.expected: Interests pull you toward an area; abilities are what you build; potential is what you could become
questions.memo: Interests = pull. Abilities = current skills. Potential = future possibility. Together they map a learner's path.

questions.question: Lerato loves animals and is good at biology. She MIGHT consider:
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato loves animals and is good at biology. What might she consider as a career?
questions.expected: Veterinarian, animal behaviourist, conservationist
questions.memo: Interest + ability = a path. Lerato's combination suggests animal-related careers. Mentors, internships and study can grow her potential.

questions.question: Sipho is great at maths and loves problem-solving. He could become a:
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho is good at maths and loves problem-solving. He could become a:
questions.expected: Engineer, accountant, software developer, scientist
questions.memo: Maths opens many doors — engineering, finance, tech, science, architecture. Sipho's combo is strong; he should pursue it.

questions.question: True or false: Potential is fixed at birth and can't change.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Potential is fixed at birth and can't change.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: Potential grows with effort, teaching and opportunity. People discover talents they didn't know they had — every day, at every age.

questions.question: What is an 'opportunity'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is an opportunity?
options: A chance to try, learn or grow toward something
questions.expected: A chance to try, learn or grow toward something
questions.memo: Opportunities are openings — a school club, an internship, a competition, a free course online. Taking them grows potential.

questions.question: Mpho wants to be a writer. Which is a real STEP she can take this year?
questions.ruby_prompt: Mpho wants to be a writer. Which is a real step she can take this year?
options: Write something short every week, join a book club, enter a writing competition
questions.expected: Write something short every week, join a book club, enter a writing competition
questions.memo: Real action grows ability. Weekly writing, reading good writers, getting feedback — these turn potential into reality.

questions.question: Why is it useful to make an ACTION PLAN for your potential?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it useful to make an action plan for your potential?
options: Plans turn vague hopes into concrete steps you can actually take
questions.expected: Plans turn vague hopes into concrete steps you can actually take
questions.memo: A vague 'I want to be X' is a dream. 'I will do A this week, B this month, C this year' is a plan. Plans get you there.

questions.question: Karabo's interest changed from drawing to coding. What's the healthy response?
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo's interest changed from drawing to coding. What's a healthy response?
options: Notice the change, explore the new interest, see if it grows or fades
questions.expected: Notice the change, explore the new interest, see if it grows or fades
questions.memo: Interests change — that's normal, especially at this age. Exploring is healthy. Some interests stick, some don't.

questions.question: True or false: You can only have ONE main ability.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: A person can only have one main ability.
questions.expected: false
questions.memo: Most people have several abilities — maths AND empathy, sport AND music, language AND science. Don't choose just one.

questions.question: Where can a young person EXPLORE their abilities and interests?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where can a young person explore their abilities and interests?
options: School clubs, libraries, community groups, free online courses, mentors
questions.expected: School clubs, libraries, community groups, free online courses, mentors
questions.memo: Many free paths exist. SA has libraries, free MOOCs (Khan Academy, Coursera basics), school clubs and community programmes.

questions.question: Put these steps in order for making an action plan for your potential.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order for making an action plan for your potential.
options: Name what interests you or what you'd like to grow
Find one small step you can take this week
Do it and notice how you feel
questions.expected: Name what interests you or what you'd like to grow,Find one small step you can take this week,Do it and notice how you feel,Plan the next step
questions.memo: Name → step → do → next step. Plans aren't about big leaps; they're about steady small actions.

questions.question: Tell me one of your interests or abilities.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one of your interests or abilities.
questions.expected: I love reading stories
questions.memo: Good answers: any honest interest (animals, music, science, cooking) or ability (drawing, helping others, sport, languages).

questions.question: Why is it good to TRY new things even if you might not be good at them?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it good to try new things even if you might not be good at them at first?
options: You discover new interests and abilities you didn't know you had
questions.expected: You discover new interests and abilities you didn't know you had
questions.memo: Hidden talents come out through trying. Many famous people 'fell into' their gift by experimenting widely.

questions.question: A 'mentor' is:
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a mentor?
options: An experienced person who guides and supports a younger person
Someone the same age as you
questions.expected: An experienced person who guides and supports a younger person
questions.memo: Mentors share their experience to speed up your learning. Teachers, family, community elders and online figures can all mentor.

questions.question: True or false: Reading widely helps you discover interests you didn't know existed.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Reading widely helps you discover interests you didn't know existed.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. Books, magazines, articles open windows on jobs and worlds you'd never encounter otherwise. Libraries are free!

questions.question: If your dream feels too big, the first move is to:
questions.ruby_prompt: If a dream feels too big, what's the first move?
options: Break it into one small step you can take this week
Wait for someone to do it for you
questions.expected: Break it into one small step you can take this week
questions.memo: Big dreams move one step at a time. Anyone who has built something big started with one Tuesday afternoon's worth of effort.

questions.question: Which is the most important truth about your potential?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the most important truth about your potential?
options: It grows with effort, learning, support and opportunity — it isn't fixed
questions.expected: It grows with effort, learning, support and opportunity — it isn't fixed
questions.memo: Potential is shaped, not given. With kind adults, real chances and your own effort, your future is genuinely open.

LS.L6.PSW.T03.title: Peer pressure
LS.L6.PSW.T03.description: Examples of peer pressure at school and in the community; appropriate responses in different situations.
LS.L6.PSW.T03.recovery_strategy: Affirm: it's normal to want to fit in. Reinforce: real friends respect a no. Practise concrete refusal lines.

questions.question: What is 'peer pressure'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is peer pressure?
options: When friends or classmates push you to do something — good or bad — to fit in
questions.expected: When friends or classmates push you to do something — good or bad — to fit in
questions.memo: Peer pressure can push us toward good things (studying, sport) or harmful ones (drugs, bullying). The key is to choose, not just follow.

questions.question: Which is an example of POSITIVE peer pressure?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is an example of positive peer pressure?
options: Friends who study together and encourage homework
Friends who tell you to skip school
Friends who tease you for being kind
Friends who pressure you to fight
questions.expected: Friends who study together and encourage homework
questions.memo: Positive pressure pulls you toward growth — study habits, sport, kindness, hobbies. Choose friends who pull you up.

questions.question: Which is an example of NEGATIVE peer pressure?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is an example of negative peer pressure?
options: Friends pushing you to lie to your parents
Friends offering to help with maths homework
Friends inviting you to play sports
questions.expected: Friends pushing you to lie to your parents
questions.memo: Negative pressure pushes you against your values — lies, harm to yourself or others. Notice it. Push back.

questions.question: Why is peer pressure especially STRONG during the school years?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is peer pressure especially strong during the school years?
options: Belonging matters a lot at this age — friends are how we figure out who we are
Peer pressure is weak in school
questions.expected: Belonging matters a lot at this age — friends are how we figure out who we are
questions.memo: It's biology. Pre-teen and teen brains are wired to care deeply about peers. Knowing this helps you not be blindsided by it.

questions.question: True or false: You can say no without losing your friends.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: You can say no to peer pressure without losing your friends.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Real friends respect a clear no. If a 'friend' rejects you for saying no to something harmful, they weren't a real friend.

questions.question: Lerato's friends want her to bunk school. What's the strongest response?
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato's friends want her to bunk school. What's the strongest response?
options: Say no clearly, suggest an after-school plan, and stick to her values
questions.expected: Say no clearly, suggest an after-school plan, and stick to her values
questions.memo: Clear + alternative is powerful. 'No, but let's meet after school' keeps the friendship and your standards.

questions.question: A short, strong refusal line is:
questions.ruby_prompt: What's an example of a short, strong refusal line you could practise?
options: 'Well, only if everyone else does it...'
'I'll do it if you keep asking.'
questions.expected: 'No thanks, that's not for me.'
questions.memo: Practised lines are easier to use under pressure. Short, firm, no apology, no long explanation. Use it.

questions.question: Sipho's classmates dare him to steal sweets from a shop. He should:
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho's classmates dare him to steal sweets from a shop. What should he do?
options: Refuse — stealing is illegal, harms the shopkeeper, and isn't worth their 'approval'
Steal only one to fit in
questions.expected: Refuse — stealing is illegal, harms the shopkeeper, and isn't worth their 'approval'
questions.memo: Theft has consequences — for the shop owner, for Sipho's record, for his own self-respect. The friends won't pay any price; he would.

questions.question: Which is a sign of an UNHEALTHY friendship under peer pressure?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a sign of an unhealthy friendship under peer pressure?
options: The friend keeps pushing past your clear no
The friend asks how you feel
questions.expected: The friend keeps pushing past your clear no
questions.memo: A real friend respects no. Pushing past it = pressure, manipulation or worse. Time to rethink the friendship.

questions.question: True or false: Choosing friends carefully reduces negative peer pressure.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Choosing your friends carefully reduces negative peer pressure.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — the company you keep shapes the pressure you face. Friends who share your values bring less negative pressure.

questions.question: Mpho's friends pressure her to wear expensive brands her family can't afford. The best response is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Mpho's friends pressure her to wear brands her family can't afford. What's the best response?
options: Be honest about her family's situation, dress her own way, find friends who don't judge by clothes
questions.expected: Be honest about her family's situation, dress her own way, find friends who don't judge by clothes
questions.memo: Real friendship doesn't depend on labels. Honesty often invites respect — and may attract better friends.

questions.question: Put these in order for handling negative peer pressure.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order for handling negative peer pressure.
options: Notice the pressure and how it feels
Leave the situation if pressure continues
Talk to a trusted adult if needed
questions.expected: Notice the pressure and how it feels,Say no clearly,Leave the situation if pressure continues,Talk to a trusted adult if needed
questions.memo: Notice → no → leave → tell. Each step gives you back control.

questions.question: Karabo's group wants her to share her exam answers. The right response is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo's group wants her to share her exam answers. What's the right response?
options: Refuse — cheating harms everyone, including those who 'win' unfairly
Share so they don't get angry
Share with only half of them
questions.expected: Refuse — cheating harms everyone, including those who 'win' unfairly
questions.memo: Cheating denies real learning. Karabo's no protects her integrity AND ironically protects her friends from coasting.

questions.question: Tell me a refusal line you could use under peer pressure.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one short refusal line you could actually use under peer pressure.
questions.expected: No thanks, that's not for me
questions.memo: Good answers: 'No thanks.' 'Not today.' 'I'm out.' 'Not my thing.' 'I'd rather not.' Practise them out loud so they come easily.

questions.question: Why might a 'safety plan' with parents help with peer pressure?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why might a safety plan with parents help with peer pressure?
options: You can call a parent to fetch you out of a tough situation — no questions asked
questions.expected: You can call a parent to fetch you out of a tough situation — no questions asked
questions.memo: Many families have an exit code — a word or call that means 'come get me'. No questions, no blame. Just safety.

questions.question: When pressure feels like a lot, you can:
questions.ruby_prompt: When peer pressure feels like a lot, you can:
options: Step away to breathe, then make a calm decision based on your values
questions.expected: Step away to breathe, then make a calm decision based on your values
questions.memo: Time slows pressure. Even 30 seconds in the bathroom or 'I need to check with mom' buys clarity.

questions.question: True or false: Standing up to peer pressure once gets easier the next time.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Standing up to peer pressure once usually makes it easier the next time.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — saying no builds the muscle. Each time you do it, your sense of yourself gets stronger.

questions.question: Sometimes peer pressure comes through SOCIAL MEDIA. Which is an example?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sometimes peer pressure comes through social media. Which is an example?
options: Trends that push risky 'challenges' or harmful behaviours
questions.expected: Trends that push risky 'challenges' or harmful behaviours
questions.memo: Online 'challenges' can be deadly. Just because something is trending doesn't mean it's safe. Critical thinking matters online too.

questions.question: Which is the most important question to ask under pressure?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the most important question to ask yourself under peer pressure?
options: 'Is this what I really want, or am I just trying to fit in?'
questions.expected: 'Is this what I really want, or am I just trying to fit in?'
questions.memo: The question pulls you back to your own self. Pressure goes external; this question brings the decision back inside.

questions.question: The strongest way to handle negative peer pressure is:
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the strongest way to handle negative peer pressure long term?
options: Build friendships with people who share your values — pressure becomes much smaller
questions.expected: Build friendships with people who share your values — pressure becomes much smaller
questions.memo: The best defence is the right offence: friends whose values match yours. Negative pressure mostly disappears in that company.

LS.L6.PSW.T04.title: Problem solving in conflict situations
LS.L6.PSW.T04.description: Keeping safe and protecting self and others; mediation skills; peacekeeping skills (acceptance, respect, co-operation, personal responsibility, listening).
LS.L6.PSW.T04.recovery_strategy: Walk through real steps for de-escalation. Reinforce: physical safety first, mediation second. Acknowledge that some conflicts need adult help.

questions.question: What is 'mediation'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is mediation?
options: When a third person helps two sides find a fair solution
questions.expected: When a third person helps two sides find a fair solution
questions.memo: A mediator listens to both sides and helps them work out an agreement. Many schools and courts use mediators.

questions.question: Which is the FIRST step in solving a conflict?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the first step in solving a conflict?
options: Calm down — both sides need to be cool enough to think
questions.expected: Calm down — both sides need to be cool enough to think
questions.memo: Hot brains can't solve problems. Calm first — breath, water, walk — then talk. Adults skip this step too often.

questions.question: True or false: Listening is half of solving a conflict.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Listening is at least half of solving a conflict.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. People who feel heard become much more willing to compromise. Real listening — not just waiting to speak — is the magic.

questions.question: An 'I-statement' helps because:
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does an I-statement help in conflict?
options: It shares your feelings without blaming the other person
It makes the other person angry
questions.expected: It shares your feelings without blaming the other person
questions.memo: 'I feel X when Y happens because Z' is the formula. Compare to 'You always...' which puts the other person on defence.

questions.question: Lerato's two friends are fighting. She wants to help as a MEDIATOR. She should:
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato's two friends are fighting. She wants to help mediate. What should she do?
options: Listen to each side separately, find common ground, suggest a fair solution
Tell them to stop being silly
questions.expected: Listen to each side separately, find common ground, suggest a fair solution
questions.memo: Good mediators are NEUTRAL. They listen to both, look for what both sides actually want, and help craft a fair middle.

questions.question: When a conflict turns PHYSICAL, the safest move is:
questions.ruby_prompt: When a conflict turns physical, what's the safest move?
options: Move away, get adult help — don't try to break it up alone
questions.expected: Move away, get adult help — don't try to break it up alone
questions.memo: Physical fights can hurt anyone who jumps in. Get help. Children should not break up fights — that's an adult's job.

questions.question: Which is a peacekeeping skill?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a peacekeeping skill?
questions.expected: Listening without interrupting
questions.memo: Peacekeeping skills: listening, respect, cooperation, taking responsibility, calm voice. Practise them in small daily conflicts.

questions.question: What does 'taking responsibility' mean in a conflict?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does 'taking responsibility' mean in a conflict?
options: Owning the part YOU played — even if the other person also played a part
questions.expected: Owning the part YOU played — even if the other person also played a part
questions.memo: Few conflicts are 100% one person's fault. Acknowledging your part — even a small part — softens the whole conversation.

questions.question: Sipho and a classmate disagree about a project. The best step is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho and a classmate strongly disagree about how to do their project. What's the best step?
options: Listen to each other, look for shared goals, and find a solution both can live with
Tell the teacher to fail them
questions.expected: Listen to each other, look for shared goals, and find a solution both can live with
questions.memo: Project conflicts are great practice. Listening + shared goals + creative middle ground = mature problem-solving.

questions.question: True or false: A good solution often means BOTH sides give a little.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: A good solution to a conflict often means both sides give a little.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Compromise is rarely a loss — it's often the start of a stronger relationship. 'Win-lose' breeds future fights.

questions.question: Which response helps DE-ESCALATE a conflict?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which response helps de-escalate a conflict?
options: Lower your voice, slow down, and acknowledge the other person's feelings
questions.expected: Lower your voice, slow down, and acknowledge the other person's feelings
questions.memo: Soft voice, slow speech, naming the other's feelings — these cool things down fast. Used by police, counsellors and good teachers.

questions.question: Mpho and her sister fight constantly about chores. A real fix is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Mpho and her sister fight constantly about chores. What's a real fix?
options: Sit down with their parents and write a fair chore roster everyone agrees to
questions.expected: Sit down with their parents and write a fair chore roster everyone agrees to
questions.memo: Repeated conflicts often need a SYSTEM, not a fight. A written chore roster takes the daily argument off the table.

questions.question: Put these in order for solving a conflict step-by-step.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order for solving a conflict step-by-step.
options: Each side speaks while the other listens
Look for what each side really needs
questions.expected: Both sides calm down,Each side speaks while the other listens,Look for what each side really needs,Agree on a fair solution
questions.memo: Calm → listen → understand needs → agree. This is the conflict-resolution backbone used worldwide.

questions.question: Karabo is being threatened by an older child. The safest response is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo is being threatened by an older child. What's the safest response?
options: Get away to safety and tell a trusted adult immediately
Try to fight the older child
questions.expected: Get away to safety and tell a trusted adult immediately
questions.memo: Threats with a power difference (size, age) need an adult. Karabo's safety is priority one. Mediation doesn't apply with bullies — adults do.

questions.question: Tell me one skill you can use to help solve a conflict.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one skill you can use to help solve a conflict.
questions.expected: Listen to the other person without interrupting
questions.memo: Good answers: listening, calm voice, I-statements, finding shared ground, compromise, asking what the other needs.

questions.question: What is 'co-operation' in a conflict?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is co-operation in a conflict?
options: Working TOGETHER to find a solution, not against each other
questions.expected: Working TOGETHER to find a solution, not against each other
questions.memo: Co-operation flips conflict on its head — instead of 'me vs you', it's 'us vs the problem'. Same brains, working together.

questions.question: Which sentence shows 'accepting differences'?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which sentence shows accepting differences?
options: 'We see this differently, and that's okay. Let's find a way forward.'
questions.expected: 'We see this differently, and that's okay. Let's find a way forward.'
questions.memo: Accepting differences doesn't mean agreeing — it means recognising the other person has their own view, and that's normal.

questions.question: True or false: Sometimes the right thing is to AGREE TO DISAGREE.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Sometimes the right thing is to agree to disagree.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — not every disagreement needs a winner. Two people can hold different views respectfully and still be friends.

questions.question: Why is 'respect' the key to conflict resolution?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is respect the key to conflict resolution?
options: When both sides feel respected, they listen more and compromise more
questions.expected: When both sides feel respected, they listen more and compromise more
questions.memo: Respect cools things down and opens minds. Disrespect — name-calling, mockery — closes the same minds you're trying to reach.

questions.question: Which is the BEST description of mature conflict-solving?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the best description of mature conflict-solving?
options: Both sides calm, listening, taking some responsibility, and finding a fair way forward
questions.expected: Both sides calm, listening, taking some responsibility, and finding a fair way forward
questions.memo: Mature problem-solving has these ingredients every time: calm, listen, own your part, work out a fair forward. Practise it daily in small ways.

LS.L6.PSW.T05.title: Self management skills
LS.L6.PSW.T05.description: Responsibilities at school and home, prioritising responsibilities, developing an activity plan for homework, chores and play.
LS.L6.PSW.T05.recovery_strategy: Self-management is a learnable skill, not a personality trait. Practise small daily routines. Praise the planning, not just the outcome.

questions.question: What is 'self-management'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is self-management?
options: Looking after your own time, tasks, and behaviour
questions.expected: Looking after your own time, tasks, and behaviour
questions.memo: Self-management is the skill of running your own life — planning, choosing, finishing. It's a life-long skill, starting now.

questions.question: Which is a SCHOOL responsibility?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a school responsibility?
options: Doing homework, listening in class, treating others kindly
questions.expected: Doing homework, listening in class, treating others kindly
questions.memo: School responsibilities are about effort and behaviour — both academic and social. Both matter.

questions.question: Which is a HOME responsibility?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a home responsibility?
options: Helping with chores, looking after younger siblings, taking care of your own things
questions.expected: Helping with chores, looking after younger siblings, taking care of your own things
questions.memo: Home responsibilities build a Functioning Family. Each person — even small children — pitches in to age-appropriate level.

questions.question: What does 'prioritising' mean?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does it mean to prioritise?
options: Deciding which tasks to do first, based on importance and time
questions.expected: Deciding which tasks to do first, based on importance and time
questions.memo: Priority = order of importance. Test tomorrow > game today. Homework due Friday > tidying drawer.

questions.question: An activity plan should include:
questions.ruby_prompt: What should an activity plan include?
options: Time for homework, chores, play and rest — a healthy balance
questions.expected: Time for homework, chores, play and rest — a healthy balance
questions.memo: A good plan has all four — work, contribute, play, rest. Skipping any of them comes back to bite.

questions.question: Lerato has 3 days of school tasks: an essay due Wednesday, maths homework daily, and a project due Friday. How should she prioritise?
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato has an essay due Wednesday, daily maths homework, and a project due Friday. How should she prioritise on Monday?
options: Start the essay first (Wednesday deadline), keep up daily maths, and spread project work across the week
questions.expected: Start the essay first (Wednesday deadline), keep up daily maths, and spread project work across the week
questions.memo: Earliest deadline first. Spread bigger tasks across days. Don't skip daily duties. This is grown-up planning.

questions.question: True or false: Sleep and play are also part of good self-management.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Sleep and play are also part of good self-management.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. Burnout is a real risk even for children. Rest and play are not extras — they're fuel for focus and creativity.

questions.question: Which is a sign of POOR self-management?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a sign of poor self-management?
options: Always rushing to do homework the night before it's due
Knowing when each task is due
questions.expected: Always rushing to do homework the night before it's due
questions.memo: Last-minute panic is a sign. It usually means weak planning + weak prioritising. Practice fixes it over time.

questions.question: Sipho keeps forgetting his homework. The best self-management fix is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho keeps forgetting his homework. What's the best self-management fix?
options: Write tasks in a diary or phone and check it every evening
questions.expected: Write tasks in a diary or phone and check it every evening
questions.memo: A simple list beats memory. Children and adults both rely on lists. Notebooks, phones, sticky notes — pick one and use it.

questions.question: Put these in order for a study session.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order for a useful study session.
options: Set a clear small goal (e.g. one chapter)
Find a quiet workspace with no phone distractions
Take a short break, then check what you learned
questions.expected: Set a clear small goal (e.g. one chapter),Find a quiet workspace with no phone distractions,Study with focus for 25–30 minutes,Take a short break, then check what you learned
questions.memo: Goal + quiet + focused chunk + break = study that actually sticks. Beats hours of distracted re-reading.

questions.question: Why is BREAKING a big task into smaller steps useful?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is breaking a big task into smaller steps useful?
options: Smaller steps feel doable; you start more easily and finish more steadily
Big tasks are easier as one chunk
questions.expected: Smaller steps feel doable; you start more easily and finish more steadily
questions.memo: Brains freeze at 'write a 10-page report'. They engage with 'list 5 main points'. Smaller = start-able.

questions.question: Mpho wants to balance homework, chores and play. Her best move is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Mpho wants to balance homework, chores and play after school. What's her best move?
options: Make a simple after-school schedule and stick to it most days
questions.expected: Make a simple after-school schedule and stick to it most days
questions.memo: A rough schedule (chores 4-5pm, homework 5-7pm, play/family 7-8pm) creates flow. 'Most days' allows life to happen too.

questions.question: True or false: It's a sign of strength to ASK for help when you're stuck.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Asking for help when you're stuck is a sign of strength.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. Asking for help isn't weakness — it's wisdom. Stuck and silent helps nobody. Stuck and asking gets you unstuck.

questions.question: Which is a way to manage SCREEN TIME well?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a way to manage screen time well?
options: Use screens after homework + chores, with time limits agreed with parents
questions.expected: Use screens after homework + chores, with time limits agreed with parents
questions.memo: Screens are powerful. Limits + after-priorities-first keeps them a tool, not a master. Honesty with parents helps.

questions.question: Karabo finds school overwhelming. She should:
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo finds school feels overwhelming. What should she do?
options: Talk to a teacher, parent or counsellor and break the work into smaller pieces
questions.expected: Talk to a teacher, parent or counsellor and break the work into smaller pieces
questions.memo: Overwhelm + silence = burnout. Overwhelm + asking for help + smaller pieces = back on track. Counsellors are free at most schools.

questions.question: Tell me one thing you can do TONIGHT to manage yourself better tomorrow.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one thing you could do tonight to manage yourself better tomorrow.
questions.expected: Pack my school bag and lay out my uniform
questions.memo: Good answers: pack the bag, write a to-do list, do homework, prep clothes, sleep early, set an alarm. Future-you will thank you.

questions.question: Which is a sign of GOOD self-management?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a sign of good self-management?
options: Most days you finish what you need to, without last-minute panic
questions.expected: Most days you finish what you need to, without last-minute panic
questions.memo: Good self-management isn't perfection — it's a steady pattern of getting things done on time, with enough rest and play in between.

questions.question: Why is taking RESPONSIBILITY for your own school work important?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is taking responsibility for your own schoolwork important?
options: Your future depends on it more than on anyone else
questions.expected: Your future depends on it more than on anyone else
questions.memo: Parents and teachers can support, but only YOU can do the learning. The earlier you own this, the further you go.

questions.question: Sipho finishes his maths first because he finds it easier. Is this good prioritising?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho finishes his maths first because he finds it easier. Is this good prioritising?
options: Not really — easier shouldn't equal first. He should prioritise by deadline and difficulty
questions.expected: Not really — easier shouldn't equal first. He should prioritise by deadline and difficulty
questions.memo: Easy-first feels good but leaves the hard stuff for tired-time. Better: a mix — start hard while fresh, finish easy later.

questions.question: The MOST important self-management habit is:
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the most important self-management habit?
options: Daily small actions — they add up much more than rare big efforts
One big effort once a year
questions.expected: Daily small actions — they add up much more than rare big efforts
questions.memo: Consistency beats intensity. 20 minutes daily for a year is far more learning than a panic week.

LS.L6.PSW.T06.title: Bullying: getting out of the bullying habit
LS.L6.PSW.T06.description: Reasons people bully; getting out of the bullying habit; where to find help.
LS.L6.PSW.T06.recovery_strategy: Framed for learners who may themselves bully. Non-shaming. Provide concrete alternatives and adult help paths. Bullying is a habit that can be changed.

questions.question: Why do people sometimes BULLY others?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do people sometimes bully others?
options: Often because they are hurting, copying others, or trying to feel powerful
questions.expected: Often because they are hurting, copying others, or trying to feel powerful
questions.memo: Bullies usually have pain behind their behaviour. That doesn't excuse it — but it explains it. Understanding helps both sides.

questions.question: True or false: A bully can CHANGE their behaviour.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: A bully can change their behaviour.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. Bullying is a habit. Like any habit, it can be unlearned — with self-awareness, support, and practice.

questions.question: What is the FIRST step in getting out of the bullying habit?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the first step in getting out of the bullying habit?
options: Admitting to yourself that what you've been doing is hurtful
questions.expected: Admitting to yourself that what you've been doing is hurtful
questions.memo: Honesty with yourself is the start. You can't fix what you won't name. Self-awareness is brave.

questions.question: Sipho realises he's been bullying a quieter classmate. What should he do?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho realises he's been bullying a quieter classmate. What should he do?
options: Stop the behaviour, apologise sincerely, and talk to a counsellor or trusted adult
questions.expected: Stop the behaviour, apologise sincerely, and talk to a counsellor or trusted adult
questions.memo: Stop → apologise → get help. A sincere apology + changed behaviour is one of the most powerful things a person can do.

questions.question: What is a healthy way to handle anger WITHOUT bullying?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's a healthy way to handle anger without bullying?
options: Talk to a counsellor, exercise, write, breathe — channel the feeling without harming anyone
Take it out on someone smaller
questions.expected: Talk to a counsellor, exercise, write, breathe — channel the feeling without harming anyone
questions.memo: Anger is normal; harming others isn't. Bullies often haven't learned healthy outlets. They can learn them.

questions.question: True or false: Bullies often feel BAD inside, even if they don't show it.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Bullies often feel bad inside, even when they don't show it.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. Bullying rarely makes anyone feel truly good. Underneath the meanness is often shame, anger or pain — and that needs care.

questions.question: Lerato keeps bullying because her group encourages it. To change, she needs to:
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato bullies because her group encourages it. To change, she needs to:
options: Step away from that group and find friends who support kinder behaviour
Stay in the group and follow
questions.expected: Step away from that group and find friends who support kinder behaviour
questions.memo: Bullying often happens in packs. Changing means leaving the pack — hard but possible. Better friends exist.

questions.question: An APOLOGY that actually helps after bullying is:
questions.ruby_prompt: What does an apology that actually helps after bullying look like?
options: Specific, sincere, no excuses, and followed by changed behaviour
questions.expected: Specific, sincere, no excuses, and followed by changed behaviour
questions.memo: Real apology: name what you did, say it was wrong, no 'but', and change what you do next. Words plus action.

questions.question: Mpho realises she's been laughing along when others bully. This makes her:
questions.ruby_prompt: Mpho realises she's been laughing along when others bully a classmate. This makes her:
options: Part of the bullying — laughing along is its own kind of harm
questions.expected: Part of the bullying — laughing along is its own kind of harm
questions.memo: Bystanders matter. Laughing or watching gives bullies energy. Stopping that participation is a real, meaningful change.

questions.question: Where can a bully find HELP to change?
questions.ruby_prompt: Where can someone who's been bullying find help to change?
options: A school counsellor, religious leader, trusted adult, Childline 116 or SADAG (0800 567 567)
questions.expected: A school counsellor, religious leader, trusted adult, Childline 116 or SADAG (0800 567 567)
questions.memo: Help is real for bullies too. Counsellors don't punish — they help people understand and change. Asking is brave.

questions.question: Why does bullying often go from generation to generation in families?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does bullying often go from generation to generation in families?
options: Children copy what they see — but they can choose to break the cycle
questions.expected: Children copy what they see — but they can choose to break the cycle
questions.memo: Cycles repeat unless someone chooses to break them. That someone could be the learner today. Massive ripple effect.

questions.question: True or false: People who bully are often also being bullied somewhere else.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: People who bully are often also being bullied somewhere else in their life.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Often true. Hurt people hurt people. This doesn't excuse the bullying — but it points to where the help is needed.

questions.question: Karabo realises she bullies online. The strongest action is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo realises she's been cyberbullying others online. What's the strongest action?
options: Stop, delete the mean posts, apologise, and talk to a parent or counsellor
Keep posting but use a fake name
questions.expected: Stop, delete the mean posts, apologise, and talk to a parent or counsellor
questions.memo: Online behaviour is real behaviour. Stopping + apologising + adult help is the way out. Posts leave records — deleting is a start, not the end.

questions.question: Put these in order for getting out of the bullying habit.
questions.ruby_prompt: Put these in order for getting out of the bullying habit.
options: Get help to keep changing — counsellor, mentor, support
questions.expected: Notice what you've been doing,Take responsibility — own it,Stop the behaviour and apologise,Get help to keep changing — counsellor, mentor, support
questions.memo: Notice → own it → stop + apologise → ongoing help. Change isn't instant. Support keeps the change real.

questions.question: Tell me one healthier thing you could do when you feel angry at someone.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one healthier thing you could do when you feel angry at someone.
questions.expected: Walk away and take deep breaths
questions.memo: Good answers: walk away, breathe, write it out, exercise, talk to a trusted adult, count to 10 backwards. Healthy = doesn't harm.

questions.question: True or false: A person who STOPS bullying and changes really has done something brave.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: A person who stops bullying and changes their behaviour has done something brave.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — it takes courage to face what you've done and change. Many adults never manage it. Doing it as a child is admirable.

questions.question: Why is REPAIRING relationships important after bullying?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is trying to repair relationships important after bullying?
options: Real change means making it right with those you harmed, where possible
questions.expected: Real change means making it right with those you harmed, where possible
questions.memo: Repair is part of justice. Sometimes the victim doesn't want contact — that's their right. But the offer matters.

questions.question: If a former bully relapses (does it again), they should:
questions.ruby_prompt: If someone trying to stop bullying does it again, what should they do?
options: Notice the relapse, take responsibility quickly, keep trying — change isn't always perfect
questions.expected: Notice the relapse, take responsibility quickly, keep trying — change isn't always perfect
questions.memo: Relapse is part of breaking any habit. The point isn't perfection — it's the direction. Keep walking back to the changed behaviour.

questions.question: Which describes a healthier version of YOURSELF after leaving bullying behind?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which describes a healthier version of yourself after leaving bullying behind?
options: Someone who builds others up, takes responsibility, and feels good about themselves
questions.expected: Someone who builds others up, takes responsibility, and feels good about themselves
questions.memo: The freed-from-bullying self gets to feel proud, build friendships, and stand tall. Bullying steals that future; stopping it gives it back.

questions.question: What's the MOST hopeful truth about bullying?
questions.ruby_prompt: What's the most hopeful truth about bullying?
options: It is a habit, not a sentence — both bullies and victims can heal and change
Some people are just born bullies
questions.expected: It is a habit, not a sentence — both bullies and victims can heal and change
questions.memo: Bullying is changeable, healable, recoverable. Both sides of the equation can grow into something better with help.

LS.L6.PSW.T07.title: Cultural rites of passage
LS.L6.PSW.T07.description: Important life stages in SA cultures — birth, baptism, wedding, death — and their personal and social significance.
LS.L6.PSW.T07.recovery_strategy: Approach all cultural rites with equal respect. Use neutral language; never rank cultures. The aim is recognition and understanding.

questions.question: What is a 'rite of passage'?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is a rite of passage?
options: A ceremony marking a major life change — birth, growing up, marriage, death
questions.expected: A ceremony marking a major life change — birth, growing up, marriage, death
questions.memo: Rites of passage mark the move from one life stage to another. They give meaning, community and identity.

questions.question: Which of these is a rite of passage in MANY cultures?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is a rite of passage in many cultures?
options: Welcoming a new baby into the family or community
questions.expected: Welcoming a new baby into the family or community
questions.memo: Birth ceremonies — baby naming, dedication, baptism — exist across cultures. They mark a new person joining the community.

questions.question: Baptism is a Christian rite that:
questions.ruby_prompt: What does baptism mean in Christianity?
options: Welcomes a person (often a baby or an adult) into the Christian community using water
questions.expected: Welcomes a person (often a baby or an adult) into the Christian community using water
questions.memo: Baptism uses water as a symbol of cleansing and new life in Christ. Different Christian traditions do it differently.

questions.question: A wedding ceremony marks:
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a wedding ceremony mark?
options: The start of a marriage between two adults — a major life and family change
questions.expected: The start of a marriage between two adults — a major life and family change
questions.memo: Weddings declare two lives joining and a new family being formed. Different cultures celebrate this with their own rituals.

questions.question: Funerals (death rites) mostly serve to:
questions.ruby_prompt: What do funerals — death rites — mostly serve to do?
options: Honour the life that was lived and help the living grieve together
questions.expected: Honour the life that was lived and help the living grieve together
questions.memo: Funerals are for the living as much as the dead — community, grief, memory, comfort. Every culture has its own funeral traditions.

questions.question: In some African cultures, ULWALUKO is:
questions.ruby_prompt: In some African cultures (like Xhosa), ulwaluko is a rite of passage that:
options: Marks a boy's traditional transition into manhood
questions.expected: Marks a boy's traditional transition into manhood
questions.memo: Ulwaluko is the Xhosa traditional male initiation — a significant rite of passage with deep cultural meaning. Done safely in formal settings.

questions.question: Among Hindu families, a Mundan ceremony often:
questions.ruby_prompt: Among many Hindu families, a Mundan ceremony often:
options: Marks a child's first haircut as a rite of passage
questions.expected: Marks a child's first haircut as a rite of passage
questions.memo: Mundan — first haircut — is celebrated as a rite of passage in many Hindu families. It marks a step toward growing up.

questions.question: Why do rites of passage MATTER for individuals?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why do rites of passage matter for individuals?
options: They give meaning, identity and community support at big life transitions
questions.expected: They give meaning, identity and community support at big life transitions
questions.memo: Major changes — birth, adulthood, marriage, death — are hard. Rites give them structure, witness and meaning. They steady the person going through.

questions.question: True or false: All cultures in SA have some form of rite of passage for major life events.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: All cultures in SA have some form of rite of passage for major life events.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — every culture marks birth, adulthood, marriage, death somehow. The forms differ; the human need is universal.

questions.question: A Jewish Bar Mitzvah or Bat Mitzvah celebrates:
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a Jewish Bar Mitzvah (boys) or Bat Mitzvah (girls) celebrate?
options: A young person taking on adult religious responsibilities, usually at 12 or 13
questions.expected: A young person taking on adult religious responsibilities, usually at 12 or 13
questions.memo: At 12 (girls) or 13 (boys), Jewish young people are recognised as adults in religious terms. SA Jewish communities celebrate this.

questions.question: When attending a rite of passage from another culture, the respectful approach is:
questions.ruby_prompt: When attending a rite of passage from another culture, what's the respectful approach?
options: Dress modestly, follow the host's lead, ask if unsure, and stay quiet during sacred parts
questions.expected: Dress modestly, follow the host's lead, ask if unsure, and stay quiet during sacred parts
questions.memo: Modesty + following the host + asking + silence during sacred moments — that's the respectful guest in any culture.

questions.question: Lerato is invited to a Muslim wedding. Which would be appropriate?
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato is invited to a Muslim wedding. Which would be an appropriate way to attend?
options: Dress modestly, follow the hosts' lead on prayer times and customs
Eat food not allowed in Islam to test
Skip the ceremony but eat the food
questions.expected: Dress modestly, follow the hosts' lead on prayer times and customs
questions.memo: Modest dress, polite questions, taking cues from the family — that's the way. Muslim weddings vary in formality but modesty is universal.

questions.question: True or false: People sometimes blend rites from more than one culture.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: People in SA sometimes blend rites from more than one culture or religion.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — many SA families mix traditions, especially when parents come from different backgrounds. Blending honours both heritages.

questions.question: Sipho's grandmother passes away. The funeral helps him because:
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho's grandmother passes away. The funeral helps him because:
options: He grieves WITH the family — meaning, ritual and community ease the loss
questions.expected: He grieves WITH the family — meaning, ritual and community ease the loss
questions.memo: Grief shared is grief lessened. Funerals draw the family together, witness the loss, and start the healing.

questions.question: Which is a COMMON theme across most cultural rites of passage?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a common theme across most cultural rites of passage?
options: Community comes together to witness and bless the change
questions.expected: Community comes together to witness and bless the change
questions.memo: Community witness is universal. Whether the rite is religious or cultural, the person being marked is held by their people.

questions.question: Why might TRADITIONAL CLOTHING be worn at a rite of passage?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is traditional clothing often worn at a rite of passage?
options: It connects the person to ancestors, history, and cultural identity
questions.expected: It connects the person to ancestors, history, and cultural identity
questions.memo: Clothing tells stories. Wedding clothes, mourning clothes, initiation clothes — each connects the moment to long-standing meaning.

questions.question: Mpho's friend invites her to a baby blessing. The polite thing is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Mpho is invited to a baby blessing. What's the polite thing to do?
options: Bring a small gift or card, dress appropriately, congratulate the family
questions.expected: Bring a small gift or card, dress appropriately, congratulate the family
questions.memo: A small gift acknowledges the moment. Polite words to the family carry the love forward. Cultural specifics vary — ask if unsure.

questions.question: Tell me one rite of passage you know of and what it marks.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one rite of passage you know of and what it marks.
questions.expected: A wedding — when two people get married
questions.memo: Good answers: birth, baptism, naming ceremony, initiation, Mundan, Bar/Bat Mitzvah, wedding, funeral, ancestor ceremony.

questions.question: True or false: Rites of passage strengthen the bond between generations.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Rites of passage often strengthen the bond between generations in a family.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. Grandparents, parents and children gathering for these moments knit the generations together. Stories pass through.

questions.question: The personal SIGNIFICANCE of a rite of passage is often:
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the personal significance of a rite of passage often?
options: A felt sense of growing up, of being part of something bigger, of being seen
questions.expected: A felt sense of growing up, of being part of something bigger, of being seen
questions.memo: When a rite is done well, the person comes away changed. They know they are growing up, that they belong, that they matter. That's the gift.

LS.L6.PSW.T08.title: Dignity of the person in religions of SA
LS.L6.PSW.T08.description: How a variety of religions in South Africa frame the dignity of the person.
LS.L6.PSW.T08.recovery_strategy: Treat every religion's view with equal respect. Focus on the shared core: every human has worth. Avoid declaring one religion right.

questions.question: What does 'human dignity' mean?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does human dignity mean?
options: The worth that every person has, simply because they are human
questions.expected: The worth that every person has, simply because they are human
questions.memo: Dignity is the worth every person carries just for being human. It can't be earned and can't be taken away.

questions.question: In Christianity, the dignity of the person comes from:
questions.ruby_prompt: In Christianity, where does the dignity of the person come from?
options: Being created in the image of God
questions.expected: Being created in the image of God
questions.memo: 'Imago Dei' — Christians teach that every person bears God's image and is therefore precious.

questions.question: In Islam, the dignity of the person is rooted in:
questions.ruby_prompt: In Islam, where is the dignity of the person rooted?
options: Every person being a creation of Allah and given honour by Him
questions.expected: Every person being a creation of Allah and given honour by Him
questions.memo: The Qur'an teaches that Allah has honoured the children of Adam — every person carries that honour, regardless of background.

questions.question: In Hinduism, the soul of every person is:
questions.ruby_prompt: In Hinduism, what is taught about the soul of every person?
options: Sacred — connected to the divine; every person carries this worth
questions.expected: Sacred — connected to the divine; every person carries this worth
questions.memo: Hindu thought teaches the atman (soul) in every person reflects Brahman (the divine). 'Namaste' means 'I bow to the divine in you'.

questions.question: In Judaism, the value of a person is taught through:
questions.ruby_prompt: In Judaism, how is the value of a person often taught?
options: 'Whoever saves one life saves an entire world' — every person carries infinite worth
questions.expected: 'Whoever saves one life saves an entire world' — every person carries infinite worth
questions.memo: The Talmud teaches that each individual person contains a whole world of possibility. Saving one = saving worlds.

questions.question: In Buddhism, the foundation of compassion comes from:
questions.ruby_prompt: In Buddhism, where does compassion for all people come from?
options: Recognising that all beings suffer and have Buddha-nature within them
questions.expected: Recognising that all beings suffer and have Buddha-nature within them
questions.memo: Buddhism teaches that all beings have the potential for awakening. This shared nature is the root of universal compassion.

questions.question: In the Baha'i Faith, all people are taught to be:
questions.ruby_prompt: In the Baha'i Faith, all people are taught to be:
options: One human family — unity is a central value
questions.expected: One human family — unity is a central value
questions.memo: Baha'is teach the unity of humankind. This central idea calls for the dignity of every person across every line.

questions.question: In African Religion, dignity is often linked to:
questions.ruby_prompt: In African Religion, dignity is often linked to:
options: UBUNTU — I am because we are; each person carries community within them
questions.expected: UBUNTU — I am because we are; each person carries community within them
questions.memo: Ubuntu is a deep African value — your humanity is bound up in mine. Dignity for one is dignity for all.

questions.question: True or false: Most religions in SA teach that every person has worth and deserves respect.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Most religions in SA teach that every person has worth and deserves respect.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. This is one of the great agreements across faiths in SA — and a foundation we can build our country on.

questions.question: Sipho's family is Christian, his friend's family is Hindu. What's a respectful approach?
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho's family is Christian; his friend's family is Hindu. What's a respectful approach?
options: Recognise both faiths value human dignity and engage with each other in kindness
Argue about whose religion is best
questions.expected: Recognise both faiths value human dignity and engage with each other in kindness
questions.memo: Friendship across faiths is part of what makes SA strong. Both families can hold their faith firmly AND respect the other.

questions.question: How does the SA Constitution support human dignity?
questions.ruby_prompt: How does the SA Constitution support human dignity?
options: It names human dignity as a founding value of our country
It says only some people have dignity
questions.expected: It names human dignity as a founding value of our country
questions.memo: Section 1 of the SA Constitution lists 'human dignity, equality and freedom' as founding values. Religion and law agree here.

questions.question: True or false: People can disagree on religion AND still respect each other's dignity.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: People can disagree on religion and still respect each other's dignity.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. Disagreement on beliefs doesn't require disrespect of persons. Most religious traditions teach exactly this.

questions.question: Which action HONOURS the dignity of another person?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these honours the dignity of another person?
options: Listening, greeting them, treating them as an equal
questions.expected: Listening, greeting them, treating them as an equal
questions.memo: Tiny daily acts — eye contact, greetings, kindness — affirm dignity. Many religions teach starting here.

questions.question: Lerato sees an older person being treated rudely. What can she do?
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerato sees an older person being treated rudely by a shopkeeper. What can she do?
options: Speak respectfully to the elder, and if appropriate, let the manager know
questions.expected: Speak respectfully to the elder, and if appropriate, let the manager know
questions.memo: Affirming dignity = stepping in with kindness. Both for the elder (a kind word) and for accountability (manager). Calm action, not violence.

questions.question: Why does the IDEA of human dignity matter for society?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why does the idea of human dignity matter for society?
options: It is the foundation for human rights, justice and peace
questions.expected: It is the foundation for human rights, justice and peace
questions.memo: If we believe people have dignity, we treat them so. Laws, schools, hospitals, friendships all rest on this idea.

questions.question: Karabo encounters a homeless person. The dignified response is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Karabo encounters a homeless person on the street. What's a dignified response?
options: Make eye contact, greet them kindly, help if she can — they are a person, not a problem
questions.expected: Make eye contact, greet them kindly, help if she can — they are a person, not a problem
questions.memo: A homeless person is a person first. Recognition — a simple greeting — affirms dignity even when material help isn't possible.

questions.question: Tell me one way that you can show respect for another person's dignity.
questions.ruby_prompt: Tell me one way you can show respect for another person's dignity today.
questions.expected: Greet them and listen when they speak
questions.memo: Good answers: greet, listen, look them in the eye, use their name, hold a door, share what you have, don't gossip.

questions.question: Across religions, what is the SHARED teaching about dignity?
questions.ruby_prompt: Across many different religions in SA, what is the shared teaching about human dignity?
options: Every person has worth and deserves respect — even those very different from us
Only people of one religion matter
questions.expected: Every person has worth and deserves respect — even those very different from us
questions.memo: On this one, almost all religions agree. It's one of the unifying ideas SA's diverse society can build on.

questions.question: True or false: Dignity is not something a person earns — it is something they HAVE.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Dignity is not something a person earns — it's something they already have.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. Dignity is inherent — born with us, not earned. This is why we don't have to 'deserve' kindness; we already do.

questions.question: If we all believed every person had dignity, what would change?
questions.ruby_prompt: If everyone genuinely believed every person had dignity, what would change?
options: Less bullying, less discrimination, fewer violations of rights, stronger communities
questions.expected: Less bullying, less discrimination, fewer violations of rights, stronger communities
questions.memo: Belief shapes behaviour. A society fully built on human dignity is gentler, fairer and braver. Each person living it brings us closer.

LS.L6.PSW.T09.title: Caring for animals
LS.L6.PSW.T09.description: Acts of cruelty to animals, taking care of and protecting animals, places of safety for animals.
LS.L6.PSW.T09.recovery_strategy: Empathy bridges between people and animals. Reinforce concrete care actions and SA's animal-protection laws (Animals Protection Act).

questions.question: Which is an act of CRUELTY to an animal?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is an act of cruelty to an animal?
options: Hitting, starving or chaining a pet for long periods
questions.expected: Hitting, starving or chaining a pet for long periods
questions.memo: Cruelty includes neglect (no food, no water, no shelter) and on-purpose harm. SA law (Animals Protection Act) punishes cruelty.

questions.question: What does a pet NEED for daily care?
questions.ruby_prompt: What does a pet need for daily care?
options: Food, clean water, shelter, exercise, attention and veterinary check-ups
questions.expected: Food, clean water, shelter, exercise, attention and veterinary check-ups
questions.memo: Animals depend on us completely. The 'Five Freedoms' include freedom from hunger, thirst, discomfort, pain, fear, and freedom to express normal behaviour.

questions.question: True or false: Animals can feel pain and fear.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Animals can feel pain and fear.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes — animals feel. Science confirms this for mammals, birds and many other creatures. Their feelings deserve respect.

questions.question: If you see someone hitting a dog, the right action is:
questions.ruby_prompt: If you see someone hitting a dog, what's the right action?
options: Don't approach the abuser; tell a trusted adult or call the SPCA
questions.expected: Don't approach the abuser; tell a trusted adult or call the SPCA
questions.memo: Personal safety first. The SPCA (Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals) can investigate and rescue. They take reports.

questions.question: What is the SPCA?
questions.ruby_prompt: What is the SPCA?
options: Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals — they protect animals
questions.expected: Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals — they protect animals
questions.memo: The SPCA exists across SA. They take in unwanted, lost or abused animals; help find homes; and investigate cruelty. Donations welcome.

questions.question: Which is a PLACE OF SAFETY for unwanted or abused animals?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which is a place of safety for unwanted or abused animals?
options: SPCA shelters, animal rescue groups, wildlife sanctuaries
questions.expected: SPCA shelters, animal rescue groups, wildlife sanctuaries
questions.memo: Shelters and sanctuaries care for animals until they find new homes — or, for wildlife, until they can return to nature.

questions.question: Lerato's family wants a pet. What should they THINK ABOUT first?
questions.ruby_prompt: Lerata's family wants a pet. What should they think about first?
options: Can they afford food, vet care, time, space for the pet's whole life?
Just the colour of the animal
questions.expected: Can they afford food, vet care, time, space for the pet's whole life?
questions.memo: A pet is a 10–20 year commitment. Money, time and space all matter. Many SA pets are abandoned when families take them on without thinking.

questions.question: True or false: Adopting from an SPCA is a way to give an animal a second chance.
questions.ruby_prompt: True or false: Adopting an animal from the SPCA is a way to give them a second chance.
questions.expected: true
questions.memo: Yes. Adopting saves a life — and sometimes two (the one you take, and the space that opens for the next animal in need).

questions.question: Sipho sees a stray dog that looks hungry and skinny. The kindest response is:
questions.ruby_prompt: Sipho sees a stray dog that looks hungry and skinny. What's the kindest response?
options: Tell an adult and contact the SPCA — don't try to handle the dog alone
questions.expected: Tell an adult and contact the SPCA — don't try to handle the dog alone
questions.memo: Stray dogs may be scared or sick. Adults and SPCA staff can help safely. Don't approach an unknown dog alone.

questions.question: Which is a cruel practice that is ILLEGAL in SA?
questions.ruby_prompt: Which of these is cruel and illegal in SA?
questions.expected: Dog fighting
questions.memo: Dog fighting causes severe suffering and is illegal under the Animals Protection Act. Reporting it can save dogs' lives.

questions.question: Why is it important to KEEP your pet's vaccinations up to date?
questions.ruby_prompt: Why is it important to keep your pet's vaccinations up to date?
options: Vaccinations prevent serious diseases that can harm the animal — and sometimes people
questions.expected: Vaccinations prevent serious diseases that can harm the animal — and sometimes people
questions.memo: Rabies, parvo, distemper — all preventable with vaccines. Some diseases (like rabies) can also pass to people. Free or low-cost clinics exist.

questions.question: Mpho's neighbours leave their dog tied up all day with no shade or water. She should:
